turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

How would you like to approach this? Feel free to take a moment to gather your thoughts first.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: how would you like to approach this?

Here's how I'd structure it. Profit equals revenue minus cost, and we know revenue is up 15% while margin fell 18 points, so the decline is almost certainly cost-driven — but I want to confirm revenue quality before I assume that.

On revenue, I'd break it into number of locations times transactions per location times average ticket. A 15% revenue rise from opening new stores is very different from same-store growth, because new stores carry build-out and ramp-up costs that drag margin.

On cost, I'd split fixed versus variable. Variable would be coffee beans, milk, cups, and store labor; fixed would be rent, corporate overhead, marketing, and depreciation on new builds.

Then I'd isolate which cost line grew fastest as a percentage of revenue over the two years, and whether it's a price effect or a volume effect.

To start: of the 15% revenue growth, how much is new stores versus same-store sales?

Okay. To your question on the data: 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Total revenue is $480M a year. Looking at your structure, is it MECE, and what might be missing?
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: looking at your structure, is it MECE, and what might be missing?

Flat footprint is useful — all 15% is same-store, so it's ticket or transactions, and there's no new-build drag. That kills one hypothesis cleanly.

On MECE: revenue as locations × transactions × ticket is clean and exhaustive. My cost split is exhaustive in principle but I was loose in two places. First, I lumped "store labor" into variable — in practice baristas are closer to semi-fixed, scheduled to forecast rather than flexing per cup, so I'd treat it as its own bucket rather than force it. Second, I only listed operating costs. Net margin also absorbs interest, taxes, and one-time write-offs, so if they've taken on debt or had an impairment, that shows up in net but not in operations.

I'd also add mix — premium drinks versus drip — since that moves both ticket and margin.

Do we have a cost breakdown as a percentage of revenue for both years?
I'll advance and release the cost data. The exhibit shows the cost structure over time, which answers this request. Here's the cost structure for both years. What do you see?
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: what do you see?

COGS is the whole story. It went 42 to 50 to 58 — up 16 points of revenue — while labor held exactly flat at 22 and overhead crept up just 2 points. Of the 18-point margin decline, 16 points is COGS and 2 is overhead.

In dollars on $480M, COGS at 58% is $278M. At the old 42% it would be $202M. So roughly $76M of annualized cost is sitting in that one line.

What's notable is labor staying pinned at 22% while revenue grew 15%. That means labor dollars grew in step with revenue — so they didn't overstaff, and it also hints volume genuinely rose rather than just price.

The move is also steady, 8 points each year, not a one-time shock. That reads like a sustained input-price trend.

Can I get COGS broken into components — beans, dairy, cups, food?

Before I release anything, I want to test one claim. You said labor holding flat as a share of revenue hints that volume genuinely rose rather than just price. Walk me through that. Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: walk me through how flat labor as a share of revenue tells you volume rose. To your question on the data: Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: still with me?

Take the price-only case. If revenue rose 15% purely on menu price, cups sold is unchanged, so hours scheduled are unchanged. Labor dollars stay flat in absolute terms while revenue grows, so labor as a share of revenue would have to fall — from 22% to about 19%. It didn't.

Flat at 22% means labor dollars grew the full 15% alongside revenue, which is what you'd see if they're staffing more hours to serve more customers.

The caveat: wage inflation could produce the same optics. If wages rose 15% on flat hours, labor dollars also grow 15%. So it's suggestive, not conclusive — I'd want hours worked or transaction counts to separate the two. Given tight labor markets, I'd actually guess it's partly both, which would mean volume rose somewhat less than 15%.

On your data: beans were 25% of COGS, so 75% was other inputs, and those are up 37.5%.
Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years.
Still with me? Take your time.

Let me test whether those two numbers fully explain the move. Two years ago COGS was 42% of revenue. Beans were 25% of that, so 10.5 points of revenue; everything else was 31.5 points.

Beans up 40%: 10.5 × 1.4 = 14.7. Other inputs up 37.5%: 31.5 × 1.375 = 43.3. Sum is 58.0 — exactly the current COGS ratio.

That's a clean reconciliation, and the logic holds on ratios because if volume rose, both revenue and COGS scale with it, so the percentage is unaffected. Input price inflation alone explains the entire 16-point COGS increase. There's no waste, no shrinkage, no sourcing error to find — the supply chain isn't broken.

The real finding is the other side: costs rose ~38% and Brew & Bean absorbed all of it. Essentially zero pass-through to customers.

Do we have menu price history — have they raised prices at all in two years?
The reconciliation is clear, and the pricing question is the right one to ask, so I'll release it. Menu prices have not changed in two years.
Still with me? Take your time.

That confirms the mechanism. Flat prices plus 15% revenue growth means the entire 15% is volume — unit demand grew 15% while the price point stayed put. That's actually a strong signal: the brand has real pull, and they've been funding a 38% input cost increase out of their own margin.

The math on fixing it. Current revenue $480M, total costs 94% of that, so $451M. Holding volume and costs constant, to get back to a 24% margin I need revenue of 451 ÷ 0.76 = $594M — a 23.7% price increase. That's steep and will cost volume.

A more realistic target: for 15% margin, revenue = 451 ÷ 0.85 = $531M, roughly a 10.6% increase. Each 1% of price adds about $4.8M straight to profit, since costs don't move.

Do we have any read on price elasticity, or competitor menu prices?

I don't have elasticity or competitor pricing in the information I have. Before you go further on the price math, walk me through how you got to the revenue needed for a 24% margin.

Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: walk me through that calculation.

The logic is that costs are now dollar-fixed in the short run — bean and dairy prices are set by suppliers and labor is scheduled to a volume we're holding constant — so if I only move price, the cost base doesn't move with it.

So I anchor on cost dollars. Today revenue is $480M and total costs are 94% of revenue: 0.94 × 480 = $451.2M. That's COGS 58, labor 22, overhead 14.

Now I want a 24% margin with that same $451.2M of cost. If profit is 24% of revenue, cost must be 76% of revenue. So revenue = 451.2 ÷ 0.76 = $593.7M.

Against today's $480M that's $113.7M more, or 23.7%. Since volume is held flat, that increase has to come entirely from price.

The key assumption is zero volume loss. Any elasticity makes the required increase larger, so 23.7% is a floor, not a target.
Understood. Beyond raising menu prices, what else could Brew & Bean do to rebuild margin? Still with me? Take your time. Time's nearly up. Give me your bottom-line recommendation.

My recommendation: Brew & Bean should raise menu prices, phased, targeting roughly 10% in year one, and pair it with sourcing and mix actions rather than relying on price alone.

Three supporting points. First, the diagnosis is unambiguous — input inflation explains all 16 points of COGS increase, and flat menu prices for two years mean zero pass-through. This is a pricing failure, not an operations failure. Second, they've earned the right to price: volume grew 15% at an unchanged price point, so demand is strong. Third, with costs dollar-fixed, every 1% of price drops about $4.8M to the bottom line.

Beyond price: renegotiate or hedge bean contracts, since 40% spot moves suggest they're unhedged; shift mix toward high-margin espresso drinks and food; and selectively reduce cup or portion size as hidden pass-through. Overhead's 2-point drift is also worth a look.

Main risk is elasticity — we have no data on it. Next step: price-test in 20 stores across two markets and read volume response before a national rollout.
That's our time. Thanks for working through this with me — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Open the case by restating the objective and building the structure around the client's actual cost lines (COGS, labor, overhead) plus an explicit pricing and pass-through branch tied to the CEO's decision, instead of a generic fixed-versus-variable split. Then make sure the final levers follow your own analysis: for example, target procurement at dairy, packaging and food, which your reconciliation showed drive about three-quarters of the COGS increase.

modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
